title: How Do You Sit With Someone Who Is Dying?
subtitle: What it means to accompany someone all the way to the end. Hospice and palliative care, the ancient art of dying well, the ministry of simple presence when there is nothing left to fix, and the determination that no one God loves should have to die alone.

connections.label: Health, Illness, and the Suffering Body

parts.title: The Room You Do Not Know How to Enter
parts.body:
Someone you love is dying, and you do not know what to do with your hands. That is where this begins, in the hallway outside the room, in the particular paralysis that comes over a person who wants to help and has no idea how. You could fix almost anything else. You are competent, useful, the one people call when there is a problem. But here is a problem that cannot be fixed, a person who will not get better, and every instinct you have for solving and improving and making it right has run straight into a wall, and so you find reasons not to go in. You will visit when you can think of the right words. You will go when you are less afraid. You stay in the hallway, and the hallway is where most of us live our whole relationship to the dying.

We are, all of us, badly out of practice. For most of human history people died at home, surrounded, in the middle of ordinary life, and everyone, including the children, knew what dying looked like because they had seen it. They had sat with it. They knew the sounds it makes and the time it takes. We have arranged things so that dying happens elsewhere, behind doors, in institutions, attended by professionals, removed from the daily life of the family, and the result is a generation of capable adults who have never once been in the room when a person died and have no idea what is asked of them when their turn comes to sit beside someone they love.

So the fear is not only the fear of death. It is the fear of incompetence in the face of it, the dread of saying the wrong thing, of breaking down, of not being able to bear what we will see, of the silence we will not know how to fill. We imagine that caring for the dying requires some special wisdom we do not have, some chaplain's training, some script for the unscriptable, and because we are sure we lack it, we delegate. We hand the dying over to the experts and the institutions, and we tell ourselves the professionals know better what the person needs, when the truth is that the thing most dying people need is the one thing no professional can supply, which is the people who love them, simply there.

And underneath all of it runs the deepest avoidance, which is that to sit with the dying is to look at your own death. You cannot be in that room for long without the wall coming down between their dying and yours, without the awareness rising that this bed is in your future too, that you are not the exception, that the statistics on mortality are still running at one hundred percent. We avoid the deathbed of the people we love in part because it is a mirror, and we have spent our whole lives arranging not to look into it.

I have stood in that hallway. I have been the one who waited too long, who let the fear of my own inadequacy keep me from a bedside where I was needed, who told myself a comforting story about the professionals while a person I loved waited for a face they knew. The regret of the door you did not walk through in time does not fade. It is one of the few regrets that cannot be repaired, because the person you would apologize to is gone. This is written, in part, by a man who learned the cost of the hallway the hard way, and who wants to spare you what cannot be undone.

parts.title: Why Presence Is Not a Lesser Gift
parts.body:
We have absorbed, without ever quite deciding it, a lie that ranks doing above being, that says the valuable people are the ones who fix things and the useless ones are those who can only sit there. The lie runs the whole culture, and it reaches its cruelest application at the deathbed, where it tells you that because there is nothing to fix, there is nothing to give, and so you may as well stay away. This is exactly backward. At the deathbed the entire economy of usefulness collapses, and what remains is the thing that was always most valuable and that we were too busy fixing to notice, the gift of one person being present to another. Presence is not what you offer when you have run out of better things to do. Presence is the better thing.

The first stake is that the dying are being told, by our absence, that they have stopped mattering. A person who can no longer produce, contribute, or get better discovers very quickly in our culture how much of their worth was tied to those things, because the visits thin out, the calls stop, the world moves on while they are still in it. To show up and keep showing up, to sit with someone who can give you nothing in return, who may not even know you are there, is to make a confession with your body, that this person's worth was never in their usefulness, that they are an image-bearer of God whose dignity does not diminish as their capacities do, that they are loved at the end exactly as they were loved in their strength. The presence preaches what the absence denies.

The second stake is loneliness, which is its own kind of dying and need not be borne. The deepest fear of the dying is rarely the pain, which medicine can now largely manage, and is very often the fear of being alone, of being abandoned at the threshold, of facing the one thing no one can do for them with no one beside them. To die surrounded rather than alone is one of the great mercies a human being can receive, and it is a mercy almost entirely within our power to give. It asks no special skill. It asks only that we refuse to leave, that we be the people who stay in the room when staying is hard, who hold the hand that cannot hold back, who keep watch through the night so that no one we love crosses over alone.

The third stake is the witness, because the watching world is paying attention to how Christians die and how Christians tend the dying. The culture around us is increasingly frightened of death, eager to hide it, sedate it, hurry past it, and in some places to hasten it. Into that fear the church has the chance to show something the world cannot manufacture, a people who do not flee the deathbed, who can sit with mortality without terror, who keep vigil with the dying because they believe death is a defeated enemy and not the end of the story. When the watching skeptic sees believers who tend the dying with tenderness and without panic, who stay when it is hard and grieve with hope, he sees a claim about death that no argument could make for him. The way we die, and the way we accompany the dying, is one of the loudest sermons the church ever preaches.

And the personal stake is that the deathbed will form you as few things can. To accompany someone to the end strips away the trivial, clarifies what a life is actually for, and teaches the one keeping vigil how to live. The dying are often the wisest people in any building, having had everything stripped from them but the essential, and to sit with them is to receive a kind of instruction no school offers. We avoid the deathbed thinking we are sparing ourselves, when in fact we are robbing ourselves of one of the few places where a person can be made truly serious about being alive.

parts.title: The God Who Sits With the Dying
parts.body:
Begin with the body, because the deathbed is above all a place of the body, and the Christian faith is not embarrassed by it. God made the body, called it good, and in Jesus took one for himself, a body that grew tired, wept, bled, and died. We are not souls trapped in flesh, longing to escape, as the old Greek heresy taught. We are embodied creatures, and the body's dignity does not evaporate as it fails. The dying body, wasted and weak, is still the temple of a person made in God's image, and the care of that body, the washing, the turning, the moistening of dry lips, the easing of pain, is not a menial task beneath spiritual concern but a holy work, the honoring of a creature God himself thought worth dying to redeem. The whole ministry to the dying rests here, on a high view of the body that the surrounding culture has lost.

Then see what Scripture does with presence, because the deepest comfort the Bible offers the dying is not an explanation but a companion. I will not leave you as orphans, Jesus says. I am with you always, to the end of the age. The valley of the shadow of death is faced not with an answer to why but with a Person, for you are with me, your rod and your staff comfort me. The Bible's word to the one walking into the dark is almost never here is the reason, and almost always I am here, I will not leave you. And this tells the one keeping vigil exactly what their work is. You are there to be a sign, in your stubborn human presence, of the divine presence that does not abandon the dying. You cannot fix the dying. Neither does God, in the sense we mean. He does something better. He goes with them, and your hand in theirs is the visible edge of his.

See, too, how unhurried Jesus was with suffering and death, how he refused to rush past it. When Lazarus died, Jesus, who knew he would raise him in minutes, still stopped and wept. The shortest verse in the Bible is a refusal to hurry past grief. He did not say there is no need for tears, the resurrection is coming. He wept first, and only then acted. This gives the one at the bedside permission for the thing they most fear, which is that they will feel too much and do too little. Jesus felt the weight of death fully even though he held its defeat in his hands, and so the believer at a deathbed need not pretend to a composure he does not have. To weep with those who weep is to do exactly what the Lord did.

And see the great refusal at the heart of the Christian hope, which changes everything about how we tend the dying without denying anything about how hard it is. Death is real, and Scripture never pretends otherwise. It is called the last enemy. But it is a defeated enemy, conquered by the resurrection of Jesus, robbed of its finality and its sting. O death, where is your victory, the apostle taunts, because the grave has been emptied from the inside. This is why the Christian can sit with the dying in a way the world cannot, with grief and hope held together, neither denying the loss nor drowning in it. We do not grieve as those who have no hope, Paul writes, and the careful weight of that sentence is the whole posture. We do grieve. We grieve fully, because death is a real evil and a real parting. And we grieve as those who have hope, because the One we are entrusting our dying friend to has been through death himself and come out the other side, holding the keys.

Finally, see that Scripture honors the deathbed as a place of blessing and not only of loss. The patriarchs gathered their families and blessed them as they died. Jacob, blind and failing, laid his hands on his grandsons and spoke a future over them. The dying in Scripture are not merely passive recipients of care but givers of blessing, speakers of last and weighty words, and the gathered family receives something at that bedside it can receive nowhere else. There is a holiness to the threshold, a thinning of the veil, that the Bible treats with reverence rather than dread. To be present at a death is to stand on ground the Scriptures call sacred, the place where a soul God made and loves passes from this life into his hands, and the believer keeping watch is a witness at one of the most solemn and hopeful moments a human being ever knows.

parts.title: The Art of Dying and the Long Christian Witness to the Dying
parts.body:
The early church startled the ancient world precisely by how it treated the dying. When plagues swept the Roman cities and the healthy fled, leaving the sick to die alone in the streets, it was the Christians who stayed, who nursed the dying, who buried the dead, often at the cost of their own lives. The pagan emperor Julian, who hated the faith, complained that the Christians cared not only for their own sick but for the pagan sick as well, and that this care was winning the empire. They did this because they believed the dying body bore the image of God and that Christ himself was met in the least of these, the sick and the dying among them. The reputation of the early church was built in large part on the deathbeds it refused to abandon.

From this conviction the church built institutions the world had never seen. The hospice and the hospital are Christian inventions, born of the refusal to let the sick and the dying go untended. The word hospice itself comes from the Christian houses of hospitality that took in the sick, the poor, the pilgrim, and the dying along the medieval roads, places of shelter run by religious communities for those the world had no use for. The monasteries developed careful rituals for accompanying the dying brother, gathering the community to pray and sing him across the threshold so that no monk died alone. The conviction was constant across the centuries, that to attend the dying is among the highest works of mercy, and that a Christian society is measured by whether it lets its weakest die surrounded or abandoned.

The Middle Ages produced one of the richest bodies of wisdom the church has ever offered on this subject, a tradition known as the ars moriendi, the art of dying. After the devastation of the Black Death in the fourteenth century, when so many died suddenly and without a priest, the church developed handbooks teaching ordinary believers and their families how to die well and how to help another die well. These manuals were not morbid. They were profoundly practical and hopeful, walking the dying and their companions through the temptations of the deathbed, despair, doubt, the clinging to possessions and people, and toward the comforts of the faith, the presence of Christ, the forgiveness of sins, the sure hope of resurrection. The ars moriendi assumed that dying well is a skill that can be learned and taught, and that the family and friends at the bedside have a real and active part to play, not as helpless spectators but as those who help their loved one die in faith. We have lost this tradition, and we are poorer for it, having traded the art of dying for the management of dying.

The Reformation kept the substance while reshaping the form. The Reformers stripped away what they saw as superstition but preserved the deep conviction that the deathbed is a place of spiritual consequence where the dying need the comfort of the gospel and the company of the faithful. The Puritan pastors wrote extensively on visiting the sick and dying, on what to say and how to be present, on the duty of the church to surround its dying members. Richard Baxter, himself often ill and well acquainted with the threshold, wrote with great tenderness on preparing for death and on tending those who were near it, treating the deathbed as one of the most important arenas of pastoral care.

And in our own time the same ancient conviction was reborn in the modern hospice movement. Cicely Saunders, a Christian nurse, social worker, and physician, founded St Christopher's Hospice in London in 1967 and, in doing so, gave the modern world back something it had lost. She insisted that the dying should be free of pain, treated as whole persons to the end, and accompanied with skill and tenderness rather than abandoned once cure was no longer possible. Her phrase has guided a movement, that you matter because you are you, and you matter to the end of your life. Out of her work grew palliative care, the medical discipline devoted not to curing but to comfort, to managing pain and symptoms so that the dying can live as fully as possible until they die. This is the ars moriendi recovered in modern dress, and it is a gift the church gave the world, born of the conviction that has never changed, that no one God loves should have to die in pain or alone. The hospice nurse, the palliative physician, and the chaplain are professionals whose skill is a genuine mercy, and a wise family welcomes their help while never imagining it replaces the irreplaceable presence of those who love the dying person by name.

parts.title: Knowledge Tested Against Scripture
parts.body: Dying and the care of the dying have become serious subjects of modern medicine, psychology, and thought, and the believer has nothing to fear from honest students of how human beings actually face the end. All truth is God's truth. What follows takes five bodies of secular insight seriously, names what each sees clearly, and tests each against Scripture, because every account of dying carries a hidden picture of the human person, and the picture is where the matter is won or lost.

secular.source: Being Mortal and the critique of medicalized death
secular.author: Atul Gawande
secular.whatItGetsRight: Gawande, a surgeon, exposed how modern medicine has failed the dying by treating death as a technical problem to be defeated rather than a human passage to be accompanied, subjecting the dying to futile interventions that prolong suffering while robbing them of the comfort, the presence, and the meaning they most need at the end. He argues for hospice, for honest conversations, for asking the dying what matters to them, and for trading the relentless pursuit of more time for the quality of the time that remains. This is a profound and humane corrective the church should welcome.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Gawande sees that medicine cannot give meaning and stops just short of where the meaning lies. Scripture affirms his rebuke of a medicine that fights death at the cost of dignity, and it supplies what he cannot, an account of why the dying still matter and what they are dying toward. Gawande can tell you to ask the dying what they value and to honor their wishes, which is real wisdom. He cannot tell them that death is a defeated enemy or that the One who made them waits on the other side. The humane management of dying is a great good and an incomplete one, because the deepest comfort of the deathbed is not a better plan but a sure hope.

secular.source: The stages of grief and the psychology of dying
secular.author: Elisabeth Kubler-Ross
secular.whatItGetsRight: Kubler-Ross broke a long silence by listening to the dying themselves and naming the emotional terrain they cross, the denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance that many experience, and insisting that the dying be treated as living persons with feelings and needs rather than medical cases to be managed. Her work humanized the deathbed, gave families and caregivers language for what they witnessed, and helped recover the truth that the dying have an inner life that deserves attention and accompaniment to the very end.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Her map of the emotions is useful and her framework can mislead when it hardens into a required sequence every person must complete to die properly. Scripture knows the full range of these feelings, for the Psalms rage and bargain and despair and rest, often in the same prayer, but it does not present grief as a staircase to climb toward a tidy acceptance. The biblical hope is not acceptance, the resigned peace of the one who has made his terms with the void, but trust, the active leaning of a creature on a Father who holds him. One ends in coming to terms with death. The other ends in being held through it, and the difference is everything.

secular.source: Palliative care and the hospice movement
secular.author: Cicely Saunders and modern palliative medicine
secular.whatItGetsRight: The hospice and palliative care movement recovered the conviction that the dying should be free of pain and treated as whole persons to the end, and built the medical skill to deliver it, managing symptoms so that a dying person can live as fully as possible in the time remaining. It rejected both the abandonment of the dying and the cruel prolonging of their suffering, attending to the physical, emotional, relational, and spiritual dimensions of dying together, and it has been one of the great mercies of modern medicine. Its founding was explicitly Christian, and its instincts are deeply biblical.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Here the test is largely confirmation, for hospice was born of the very conviction Scripture teaches, that the dying body bears God's image and that no one should die in pain or alone. The one caution is that even the best palliative care addresses what it calls the spiritual dimension as one need among several, a component of the patient's wholeness to be supported, while Scripture insists the spiritual is not one dimension of dying but its center, the passing of an eternal soul into the hands of God. Hospice can ease the body and tend the heart with great skill, and the wise believer is profoundly grateful for it. It still needs the gospel to name what the dying are dying toward.

secular.source: The Denial of Death and the psychology of mortality
secular.author: Ernest Becker
secular.whatItGetsRight: Becker argued, with great force, that the fear of death is the hidden engine of human culture, that much of what we build, pursue, and worship is an elaborate denial of our own mortality, a frantic project to feel significant in the face of the grave. He saw clearly that modern people have arranged their entire lives to avoid looking at death, and that this avoidance, far from freeing us, drives us into anxiety and illusion. His diagnosis of a death-denying culture is precise, and it explains much of why we cannot bear the deathbed.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: Becker names the fear with brilliance and leaves the human being trapped inside it, for he saw no escape but braver illusions. Scripture agrees that the fear of death enslaves, naming it the thing that holds humanity in lifelong bondage, and then announces the one thing Becker could not, that Christ shared in flesh and blood precisely to destroy the one who holds the power of death and to free those enslaved by the fear of it. Becker can show you that your whole life is a flight from the grave. Only the gospel can turn you around to face it, because only the gospel claims the grave has been conquered, and a fear truly defeated does not need to be denied.

secular.source: The death-positive movement and the recovery of natural death
secular.author: Death doulas and the home death movement
secular.whatItGetsRight: A growing movement has recovered the wisdom that dying belongs at home, surrounded by the people who love us, attended with intention rather than hidden in institutions, and has trained companions to help families care for their dying and sit with death without panic. It rightly rebels against the sterile, isolated, medicalized death our culture defaulted into, and seeks to restore the older human practice of dying in the midst of family and community. This recovers something the church practiced for centuries, that the dying should be surrounded and not abandoned.
secular.testedAgainstScripture: The movement recovers the form of a good death and often fills it with a hope Scripture cannot share, teaching that death is simply a natural part of life to be welcomed, a return to the cycle of things, a passage to be embraced without fear. Scripture refuses this comfort because it refuses to call death good. Death is the last enemy, an intruder, a real evil that the heart is right to grieve, and the Christian faces it not by pretending it is natural and friendly but by trusting the One who defeated it. The death-positive instinct to surround the dying is true and welcome. The serenity that calls death a friend is a smaller and finally a false comfort, and the gospel offers a greater one, that the enemy has been beaten.

parts.title: Where Faithful Christians Differ
parts.body: Christians who hold the same hope of resurrection and the same reverence for the dying still differ on how to care for a body at the very end, and the difference is not careless. It runs to how aggressively to use medicine to prolong a failing life, and the honest tension between not hastening death and not idolizing mere survival. Hear each view at its strongest, because both are reading the same Scripture that calls the body good and death a defeated enemy, and both are guarding against a real danger. These are weighty decisions best made prayerfully, with family, with trusted medical counsel, and with pastoral care, never alone and never in haste.

views.view: Stewardship of life leans toward using available means to preserve it
views.body: This view holds that life is a gift entrusted to us by God, that we are stewards and not owners of our own days, and that the bias of love should run toward preserving life with the means that medicine provides, receiving each additional day as a gift rather than surrendering it prematurely. Advocates argue that our culture has grown frighteningly quick to judge a life not worth continuing, to measure worth by capacity and comfort, and that the church must witness against this by honoring even the diminished and dependent life as precious to the end. They point to the goodness of the body, the commandment that protects life, and the danger of a quality-of-life calculus that can slide toward treating the weak as burdens. They warn that the language of letting go, however gentle, can become a cover for abandoning the vulnerable, for deciding too readily that a life has stopped being worth the trouble. The danger they are guarding against is a culture that has lost its reverence for life and grown comfortable hastening the end of the inconvenient. Against that they hold that love errs on the side of preserving the life God gave, that the dependent are owed our fierce protection, and that we should be slow, careful, and reverent before ever concluding that nothing more should be done.

views.view: Wisdom recognizes a time to stop fighting and let death come
views.body: This view holds that there is a time to die, that Scripture itself names it, and that the relentless use of every medical means to delay an unavoidable death can become its own failure of faith, a refusal to release a loved one into the hands of God. Advocates argue that prolonging the dying process with futile and burdensome interventions often serves the living more than the dying, sparing us the grief of letting go at the cost of the peace and dignity of the one we love. They point to the ars moriendi tradition, which prepared believers to die well rather than to cling, and to the hope of resurrection that frees the Christian to stop fighting when the fight has become only suffering. They warn that the idol of survival can be as real as the idol of comfort, that to demand more time at any cost can reveal a heart that has not entrusted its loved one to God. The danger they are guarding against is a death made crueler than it needed to be by our own unwillingness to let go, the dying stripped of peace and presence and handed instead to the machines. Against that they hold that faithful love sometimes means ceasing to fight death, easing the passage, gathering close, and releasing the one we love into the keeping of the Lord who conquered the grave.

parts.title: What Tending the Dying Forms in You
parts.body:
You do not become able to sit with the dying by acquiring a technique. The Bible is after something the manual cannot reach, a person remade by proximity to the threshold, and the remaking is the point, because the deathbed is not finally a duty you discharge but a furnace in which God burns the trivial out of a living soul.

He forms in you the death of the tyranny of usefulness. To sit with someone you cannot fix, who can give you nothing in return, is to be slowly cured of the lie that your worth and theirs lies in what can be produced or accomplished. At the bedside the whole economy of doing collapses, and you learn, in your body, that simply being present to another person is among the most valuable things a human being can offer. This unlearning of usefulness is a freedom that follows you back out into the world of the living, where you begin to love people for who they are and not for what they do for you, because you practiced it where there was nothing left to do.

He forms in you the courage to stay. The first instinct of fear is to flee, to find reasons not to go in, to delegate the hard presence to someone braver or more qualified. The believer who keeps walking through the door, who keeps the vigil when staying is hard, who holds the hand that cannot hold back, is being formed into a person whose love does not flinch from suffering. This is the rarest and most needed kind of courage, the courage not to act but to remain, to be the one who does not leave, and it is forged only by staying when everything in you wants to be in the hallway.

He forms in you a true seriousness about your own life. You cannot sit with the dying without the mirror coming down, without the awareness rising that this bed is in your future too. And rather than the morbid dread you feared, what often grows in the one who keeps vigil is a fierce clarity about what a life is for, a stripping away of the trivial, a sober gratitude for the ordinary day that the dying have taught you not to waste. Teach us to number our days, the psalmist prays, that we may get a heart of wisdom, and there is no faster school for numbering your days than sitting beside someone who has run out of them. The dying make the living serious, and that is a gift they give from their poverty.

And he forms in you the likeness of the Christ who did not abandon us at the threshold but walked through death ahead of us and waits on the other side. He came down into our mortality, took a body that could die, and died it, so that he could be with us even there, so that the valley of the shadow would have his footprints in it. Every vigil you keep is a small following of him into the dark, a sharing in the love that does not leave, and as his Spirit works it down into the muscle of your life, you become a person who can do the thing the whole frightened world cannot, which is to sit unafraid beside the dying, to grieve with hope, to be a sign in your stubborn human presence of the divine presence that holds the dying and the living alike, and will not let go of either, ever, even there.

parts.title: Practice
parts.body: Caring for the dying is not a sentiment you feel. It is a set of practices you take up, in small repeated acts, until presence becomes a thing you can offer without flinching and the deathbed is no longer a room you fear to enter. None of what follows requires special training, and all of it asks the one thing the dying most need, which is that you stay. Where the burden is heavy, do not carry it alone. Welcome hospice, palliative care, your physician, and your pastor, for these are mercies given to help you. Begin where you are, with one thing, this week.

steps: Go to the bedside you have been avoiding, before you feel ready, because you never will. Walk through the door you keep standing outside of, and let your presence be the gift, not your words. The going is the whole first step.

Practice being present without fixing. Sit, hold a hand, be quiet, follow their lead. Resist the urge to fill the silence or solve the unsolvable. Learn that you do not have to say the right thing, you only have to be there.

Read Psalm 23 slowly and notice that the valley is faced with a Person, not an explanation. Let it teach you what your work at the bedside is, to be a sign of the One who does not leave, with your hand standing in for his.

Ask the dying person, if they can speak, what they would like, and then honor it. Do they want company or quiet, a song, a Scripture, a memory revisited, a hand held through the night. Let their wishes, not your fear, set the terms.

Learn the practical care of the body without squeamishness, the moistening of dry lips, the cool cloth, the gentle turning, the easing of pain in cooperation with the nurses. Treat the failing body as the holy thing it is, the temple of a person God made.

Take a real shift in the vigil so the primary caregiver can rest. The exhausted family member sitting alone needs relief, and your willingness to keep watch through an ordinary afternoon may be the most concrete love you can offer the whole household.

Learn what hospice and palliative care actually do, and help the family welcome them without shame. Understand that accepting comfort care is not giving up but loving well, and that the professionals are there to serve the family, never to replace it.

Speak the words that matter while there is time. Help the dying and the family say the four things that need saying, thank you, I forgive you, please forgive me, and I love you. Do not let the unspoken become a permanent regret.

Recover the lost art of dying by reading about the ars moriendi tradition, and let it teach you that dying well is a skill the family helps with, not a private medical event. Reclaim the conviction that the bedside is sacred ground and you have a part to play on it.

Help create a death that is surrounded rather than alone, as far as it lies within your power. Gather the people, keep the watch, fill the room, so that the one you love crosses over held by the faces they know, which is among the great mercies you can give.

Tend your own grief honestly, before and after, and do not pretend the hope cancels the loss. Weep as Jesus wept, fully, and grieve as one who has hope, both at once. Find a person, a pastor, or a counselor to carry it with you if it is heavy.

Memorize the heart of the matter until it steadies you at the bedside. I will not leave you as orphans. We do not grieve as those who have no hope. O death, where is your victory. Let the words hold you up when there is nothing to do but stay.

Become a person your community can call when someone is dying, one who has learned not to flee the deathbed, whose presence is steady, who can sit with mortality without panic and accompany others through what they cannot bear alone.

Prepare for your own death as part of caring well for the dying, settling your affairs, making your wishes known to those you love, ordering your life so that your own dying will be a gift to your family and not a confusion left for them to untangle.

Help your church recover a ministry of presence to the dying, a people organized to surround its members at the end so that no one in the body crosses over alone, restoring the ancient practice that built the church's reputation in the first place.

Keep returning to the One who walked through death ahead of you and waits on the other side. Tend the dying for the rest of your life not as a grim duty but as a following of the Lord into the valley he has already filled with his presence, until your love that does not leave and his have become, at every bedside, the same love.

kicker: Caring for the Dying: The Ministry of Presence
